messages.subject_clean: Changing behavior of obj function values
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm starting to explore TMB and came across the following:

1. Create an obj with MakeADFun()
2. Check values of obj$fn(), obj$gr(), etc
3. After optimization, this values change, since, as I understand, the value of obj$env$last.par gets updated, and those functions are evaluated at last.par

So far as I can understand, this happens because obj$env is an environment and can be dynamically changed. Ok, but as I was exploring, sometimes I use numDeriv functions, such as grad() and hessian() to understand some calculations. So, when I use, e.g.,

numDeriv::grad(obj$fn, obj$par)

to compare with obj$gr(), the value in obj$env$last.par changes and that affect all other things we can do with obj functions.

As an example, please see the following (rendered) script at: http://leg.ufpr.br/~fernandomayer/misc/tmbexample.html. This is a very simple example where this behavior happens, and the differences there are very small, but I've seen other examples where the difference in obj$env$last.par (compared to opt$par, for example) after calling some numDeriv function was significantly different.

So, I understand that obj$env$last.par is dynamically modified, but can numDeriv (or other packages) functions also modify it? If so, what is the recommendation to avoid this pattern?

Also, how can I know how exactly this "dynamical" change in obj$env$last.par happens? I tried to find something in the documentation but was not successful.

Thanks in advance,

---

Cheers.

messages.body_plain:
I've got a multistock hierarchical surplus production model that I'm revising for some paper edits from a reviewer, and I've managed to really reduce the model performance. I'm having some real issues finding the cause of my model's instability and I was hoping the community could help.

I've attached the model code, some simulated data and a simple grid search profiling script to check parameter regions. If someone has the time and inclination to check through my code for something I'm missing, I'd be grateful. There are some switches in the first 25 lines of ProfileModel.R that will change settings (single/multi-stock, random vs fixed effects, grid size).

If you go looking: Please ignore the correlation matrix code and Inverse Wishart prior, I've simplified away from this during the search for my errors.

Thank goodness for git!

Details:

Basically, whenever I integrate over the yearly process errors as random effects, I get NaN gradient evaluations in about 50% of simulated data sets, which I think is unacceptable for a sim-est paper. This is way up from <10% of cases in the original submission.

I've tried running the model with the process errors as fixed effects, and the model converges every time. I've tried jittering starting values, increasing biomass and productivity initial parameter values, and starting the integration from the estimated optimum with all fixed effects, and I can't improve the convergence rate.

I replaced all my hand-coded negative log likelihood with TMB's canned R-style probability density functions, hoping this would smooth it out. No dice.

I've pored over this for a few days now, and I can't see any glaring errors (taking logs of negative numbers, dividing by zero, non-smooth likelihood functions). My hypothesis is that it's coming from a discontinuity caused by the posfun style clause in lines 171-175 of msProd.cpp, as this could cause something of a discontinuity in the likelihood function.

Thanks!
Sam Johnson
PhD Candidate, Simon Fraser University

Sam

messages.body_plain:
For anyone who's interested, the issue was two pronged. I had moved away from the differentiable posfun() in my search for a better estimator, which was one source of discontinuities, and there may have been some chaotic behaviour thanks to the 'explicit form' discretisation of the Schafer model, which would also cause numerical issues that acted like discontinuities.

The latter problem is related to the relative size of the time step and the r (productivity) value, making this more of a modelling/numerical issue than a TMB issue.

I think both issues were in some part responsible, as testing either fix on their own doesn't remove errant behaviour of the model completely

Thanks to Cole Monnahan for pointing out that my path had taken me away from differentiability, which would of course have issues during the integration.

Thanks also to John Sibert for pointing out the chaotic behaviour possibility. The basic idea is that high values of r can produce chaotic behaviour when the time-step is too long. To ameliorate this, I reduced the simulated r value by 50% for my simulation experiments, and added a time-step length parameter to step through years in smaller increments.

Updated model code is attached for anyone that's interested. I'll be tidying up my git repo and making it public once I have these paper revisions complete.

I've added a note to the documentation (?MakeADFun) that one should not rely upon the default arguments of any of the model object functions.
Always use explicit function arguments:

numDeriv::grad(obj$fn, obj$par)
obj$gr(obj$par)

The last.par default was mainly intended for the following construct:

obj$fn(opt$par)  ## Get likelihood and update internal 'last.par'
obj$gr()         ## Gradient for opt$par
obj$he()         ## Hessian for opt$par
obj$report()     ## Report for opt$par

Given the confusion it generates I admit the last.par default might have been a bad decision. However, it's not going to change...

Hello! I'm brand new to glmmTMB, so sorry if there are obvious responses what I've written below—I would really appreciate some help, though!

I have been using glmmTMB to run glms on a number of different measures from the same dataset (mostly count data, some of it zero-inflated, and also one doubly-bounded continuous measure). I've been sanity-checking against descriptive plots and results from linear regression, which I'm much more familiar with. Generally the outcomes seem sensible. However, the estimates I'm getting for my zero-inflated models sometimes look strange to me. For example, here are the ZI estimates for one of my models:

Zero-inflation model:

(Intercept)               1.3122     0.8531   1.538   0.1240

I(stthr.std^2):nsk.std -151.6625    67.4473  -2.249   0.0245 *

The ZI estimates seem pretty wacky to me. This is from a zero-inflated negative binomial model of (whole) minutes of speech directed to children per hour (i.e., round(tds_mph,0)). The predictors in the ZI model include household size (hsz.std), number of speakers present in the clip (nsk.std), and squared hour of day of the clip (stthr.std), plus some interactions of those. Household size and number of speakers are standardized variables ((x-m)/sd) and hour of day is centered on noon, then limited to [-1, 1]: ((hr-12)/12). The full model is specified as follows (chiyt.std = standardized child age in months; mated.bi.std = maternal education factor with two levels; chi_id = child id number):

quantity.rand <- read_csv("glmmTMB_nbinom1_largeZIestimates.csv <https://www.dropbox.com/s/i6lyh7vkv4bnybr/glmmTMB_nbinom1_largeZIestimates.csv?dl=0>") # minimal dataset at the linked URL

                           tchiyr.std + mated.bin +
                           hsz.std + nsk.std +
                           I(stthr.std^2) +
                           tchiyr.std:mated.bin +
                           tchiyr.std:nsk.std +
                           tchiyr.std:hsz.std +
                           tchiyr.std:I(stthr.std^2) +
                           (1|chi_id), # max*
                         data=quantity.rand,
                         ziformula=~I(stthr.std^2)*hsz.std + I(stthr.std^2)*nsk.std,
                         family="nbinom1")
# Notes:
# *: no cnvgnce w/ by-child slopes of I(stthr.std^2) added

Any ideas about what's going on? In playing around the the package, I've noticed some other funny behavior, such as:
- getting NAs for AIC/BIC/logLik/deviance estimates without any warning or error thrown and
- getting NAs for the (conditional) model estimates without any warning or error thrown

I assumed in those cases that I was using too complex a model and, indeed, simplifying the model often gets rid of the NAs. But now I'm faced with this other issue of the super big ZI estimates. Any and all ideas are welcome, and please let me know if you need more info! I'll copy the full model summary below.

Thanks very much in advance for any insights you can give!
Marisa

messages.body_plain:
Hi there I have 2 questions to the group,

Firstly
- is C++ 11 compilation flag allowed? I was getting errors saying

I get two warnings/errors that I think suggest we don't

"'auto' changes meaning in C++11; please remove it"

"range-based 'for' loops are not allowed in C++98 mode"

that was for a loop structured as

for(auto& val : vector_of_values

Secondly

I am doing inversions and determinants of large-ish matricies, the code I am bringing across used the eigen library like below,
Determinant
  PartialPivLU<Matrix<double,Dynamic,Dynamic>> lu(M);
  auto& LU = lu.matrixLU();
  double c = lu.permutationP().determinant(); // -1 or 1

and for the inversion

  V_invert = Vmat.llt().solve(MatrixXd::Identity(N_bins - 1, N_bins - 1));

I went down that road because in the eigen information it says "If your matrix is of a very small fixed size (at most 4x4) this allows Eigen <https://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/namespaceEigen.html> to avoid performing a LU decomposition, and instead use formulas that are more efficient on such small matrices."
Which I took as if your matrix is bigger than 4x4 don't use the matrix.inverse() or matrix.determinant() and use the decomposition methods.

So my question is what is the most efficient/fastest method to calculate inverses and determinants of matrices larger than 4x4 <Type> in TMB?

Cheers,
Craig
